title: Author's camping trip inspired Hollywood film Wicker
content:
An author who was inspired to write a short story after seeing wicker sculptures on a camping trip has said she never imagined it would become a raunchy A-list feature film.
Ursula Wills from Stroud, in Gloucestershire, had just returned from a holiday in Cornwall in 2006 when she wrote The Wicker Husband, which follows an ostracised fisherwoman who pays a basket-maker to weave her a husband.
The story was picked up by writers who "livened it up" for the big screen to become Wicker, starring Olivia Colman, Alexander Skarsgård and Peter Dinklage.
Wills called it a "unique and amazing" film that she thinks "audiences are going to go crazy for".
The author, who completed a Master of Arts degree at Bath Spa University in 2004, and spent 19 years living in Bristol, drew inspiration for the 14-page story on a camping trip.
"I'd visited this place called Melinsey Mill, which is an old watermill, where a basket maker had created an art trail around the pond, with big wicker sculptures like a stag, a giant spider, and a wicker man fishing, and I thought what would anyone want a wicker man for?" she said.
"I had the idea for the story straight away."
Wills posted The Wicker Husband on a short story website called East of the Web.
After racking up interest from readers, she was contacted by actor Rhys Jennings who, alongside Olivier Award–winning composer Darren Clark, created a musical.
In March 2020, it opened at Watermill Theatre in Newbury, but after only four nights the theatre had to close because of the Covid-19 pandemic.
A year later, she was approached by producer Justin Lothrop who asked her for film rights.
"I had a meeting with writers and directors, but after Olivia Colman came onboard in 2023 things rolled out really fast," Wills said.
"By the end of 2024 I was out in Budapest where the film was being shot.
"When I read the script, I thought it was going to be good, and when I saw it being shot in Hungary I knew it - the end result is something unique and amazing.
"I think audiences are going to go crazy for it."
Wicker, which opens in UK cinemas on 30 October and has been described as a raunchy fantasy rom-com, has garnered lots of attention online and spawned countless viral posts .
Although Wills has said the finished film remains faithful to her original short story, the intimate relationship between the fisherwoman and her wicker husband has been embellished to "liven it up".
Joint writer-directors Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson said they "loved it immediately".
"It was very sort of sparsely written, but just had these beautiful little clues throughout that suggested to us what the tone of the film could become," they explained.
"We realised this was more than a period fable. We immediately saw a satirical comedy about sex and marriage, a unique visual spectacle, and a strange love story that would ground it all."

final_quality.reason: The article reports a unique and unusual inspiration story that highlights the creative process behind a Hollywood film, providing a clear reason for readers to care about the author's journey and the making of the film.

title: Spotify uploads lyrics for Dolly Parton's Welsh version of Jolene in Irish
content:
The lyrics to Dolly Parton's Welsh version of her hit Jolene were uploaded mistakenly to Spotify in Irish.
The song was recorded before her death on 25 August , and is a collaboration with Welsh singer-songwriter Bronwen Lewis as well as Parton's niece, Jada Star.
The version has parts of the song sung in English and Welsh -  but the lyrics presented on the digital audio streaming service Spotify actually showed the language as Irish.
Spotify removed the Irish lyrics after the BBC approached it for comment.
The BBC asked Spotify when the single and lyrics were uploaded, when the error was noticed and when it will be replaced, but did not receive a response.
The single came out on 9 October , and is the second posthumous release from Parton - who was of Welsh descent.
The legendary country artist won 10 Grammy awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote more than 3,000 songs after a career spanning seven decades.
Jolene was released in 1973, and is about the fear she might lose her husband Carl Dean to a red-headed bank clerk who had flirted with him early on in their marriage .
It was was nominated for a Grammy in 1974, gave Parton her second number one single on the Billboard Hot Country Singles chart and her first foray into the main Hot 100 chart (60).
It has since had more than one billion streams on Spotify, and many famous singers have gone on to cover Jolene.
The Welsh version of the song came about after Lewis, from Neath, had translated the country classic and posted it on social media.
Then Star, Parton's niece, reached out and suggested recording Jolene in Welsh with Lewis - and Parton joined too.
In 2008, during a concert at the Cardiff International Arena, Parton reportedly revealed her Welsh ancestry to fans in the crowd.
Star revealed one side of the family from Parton's mother Avie Lee Owens was initially believed to have come from Conwy.
Following the singer's death, research by staff at Conwy council's archives suggested Parton's ancestors were from Machynlleth, in Powys, not Conwy as previously thought.

final_quality.reason: The article reports a substantive and unique development in the entertainment category, providing new information about the release of Dolly Parton's Welsh version of Jolene on Spotify and the mistake with the lyrics. The story has cultural and historical significance, highlighting Parton's Welsh ancestry and the collaboration with Welsh singer-songwriters. The mistake and its correction are also newsworthy, as they involve a popular streaming platform and a beloved artist.

title: Italian-themed festival applies for Richmond event
content:
A family-friendly Italian-themed festival could take place in south-west London in June.
Sicilian-themed Marzamemi Festival has applied for a three-day event on Richmond Green from 25 June, offering live Italian music, banquets and food stalls, cooking workshops, wine tasting, craft classes, shopping and children's activities.
The plan was welcomed by some but received 45 objections over concerns of noise and restricted access to the park.
Event founder Emily Ceraudo said it would be a "boutique, family-friendly celebration" that supported local businesses. It was previously held in Old Deer Park.
Robert Tuday, representing The Richmond Society, told Richmond Council's licensing hearing on Monday that he objected to taking away "public access to a large area of Richmond Green for a substantial period, to the point of constituting a public nuisance".
Katie Mansfield, lead member for Richmond town centre, said she did not believe the green was the right location for an event of "this scale or format".
Other residents backed the plans, with 10 letters of support.
Local mother and business owner Tara Stevens told the hearing: "We are begging for more activities like this, that are super-curated for young families, to be closer to home."
Under the plans, the 4,999-capacity event would occupy slightly more than a third of Richmond Green, and performances would take place inside marquees.
It would end by 21:00 BST on 25 and 26 June, and 19:00 BST on 27 June, with entry free for children.
Ceraudo added: "It's very much a family-friendly festival… it's at the forefront of the design of the event strategy."
Richmond's licensing committee will make a decision in the coming days.

final_quality.reason: The article provides a substantive development in the entertainment category, specifically a local event that has garnered both support and objections. The article provides a clear reason for readers to care, as it highlights the potential impact on the community and the event's design to be family-friendly.
